rv.q: Power doesn’t give any easy answers about how to feel about Kurtis, nor about what his future looks like, and Delaney gives a haunting performance of a man splintering from shame.
Scratch that surface and it's got a core of steel - an unflinching look at the human condition that's only cosplaying as cute.
Power's play is a rich, narrative-driven look at the obstacles standing in the way of rehabilitation initiatives.
Welcome to Pemfort is most definitely one such play
Power’s script brilliantly tackles big themes of violence, shame, guilt and responsibility in a genuinely engaging way.
Welcome to Pemfort is a tremendous piece of theatre, and one that completely hits its intentions.
It's rare to find writing of this calibre on the fringe.

The early scenes are short and rather awkwardly spliced together, tending to start and end abruptly. But there’s a smattering of decent gags – such as when Uma breezily tells the woefully under-trained Kurtis he’s suffering from “imposter syndrome” – and the overall air is of Black Books crossed with Ghosts.
Despite its central moral dilemma, and some comic moments, the play is a bit too superficial for its content.

cn.t: A deceptively gentle comedy about a castle gift shop that takes a powerful tonal shift to tackle questions of guilt and forgiveness. Critics praise Power's shattering script and nuanced performances.
